resources.string: New Caledonia parasitic yew
Parasitaxus usta
parasitic yew
A root-parasitic conifer attached to Falcatifolium taxoides. Flattened branchlets bear tiny opposite leaves, often purple; it forms no independent roots.
Endemic to New Caledonia in humid forests where its host grows.
Low parasitic shrub, generally under 2 m, with dense upright branchlets.
Scale leaves opposite and decussate, appressed to branchlets.
Small reproductive cones on branchlets; the local flora source describes the species as monoecious.
Seed surrounded by a fleshy red aril at maturity.
Five-veined trevoa
Trevoa quinquenervia
trevoa
Chilean shrub of dry slopes, recognized by spiny branches and opposite leaves with five or seven prominent veins. Whitish flowers develop into hairy achenes.
Endemic to central Chile in dry scrub and rocky habitats.
Branched shrub 0.5–3 m tall; opposite branchlets end in spines.
Leaves opposite, small and elliptic, with 5–7 longitudinal veins; underside sometimes hairy.
Small whitish flowers in axillary clusters.
Flattened, dry, hairy achene with a short beak.
Rehder’s hop-hornbeam
Ostrya rehderiana
Rehder hop-hornbeam
Very rare tree of Tianmu Shan, related to hop-hornbeams. Doubly serrate leaves and fruits enclosed in inflated papery bladders are distinctive.
Endemic to the Tianmu range, Zhejiang, eastern China; montane forest.
Deciduous tree reaching about 20 m.
Alternate elliptic leaf, sharply doubly serrate, with 13–16 pairs of lateral veins.
Male flowers in hanging catkins; female flowers develop into fruit clusters.
Small nut enclosed in a papery bladder-like husk with a stalked base.
Cottendorfia
Cottendorfia florida
cottendorfia
Large terrestrial bromeliad of Brazil’s campos rupestres. It forms a rosette of narrow leaves and a highly branched inflorescence bearing dense spikes.
Northeastern Brazil, on rocky ground in Piauí and Bahia.
Perennial rosette; the flowering stalk may bring the plant to 2–4 m.
Strap leaves up to 1 m × 1.2 cm, entire, scaly beneath.
Loose tripinnate inflorescence with compact spikes of six-parted flowers.
Dry capsule developing after flowering.
Glabrous marsh pitcher plant
Heliamphora glabra
glabrous heliamphora
Carnivorous plant of the wet Guiana Highlands. Pitcher leaves trap arthropods; a nectar-bearing appendage helps distinguish its pitchers in the genus.
Guyana and neighboring Guiana Shield areas; very wet tepuis.
Perennial pitcher rosettes with a flowering scape above the traps.
Leaves modified into upright tubular pitchers, open at the top and bearing a nectariferous appendage.
Few flowers per scape, with white floral parts and numerous stamens.
Seed capsule; pitchers are leaves, not fruits.
Travancore garcinia
Garcinia travancorica
Travancore garcinia
Tree endemic to the southern Western Ghats. Opposite leathery leaves accompany unisexual flowers and a large fleshy berry.
Evergreen wet forests of the southern Western Ghats, India.
Evergreen tree about 10–15 m tall; the consulted flora describes separate male and female flowers.
Leaves opposite, narrowly elliptic to lanceolate, leathery, sometimes with revolute margins.
Unisexual axillary flowers; four petals are reported by the consulted source.
Fleshy berry about 3–4 cm, with persistent sepals and stigma.
Umbellate miersiella
Miersiella umbellata
umbellate miersiella
Tiny achlorophyllous mycoheterotrophic herb dependent on soil fungi. Its pale stem bears scales and a terminal umbel.
Tropical wet forests of Colombia and adjacent regions, in shaded leaf litter.
Inconspicuous herb only a few centimeters tall, without independent photosynthesis.
Leaves reduced to small translucent scales along the stem.
Terminal umbel of a few minute whitish flowers.
Capsule with minute seeds; the plant remains dependent on soil fungi.
Alpine rose
Rosa pendulina
Alpine rose
Wild mountain rose, often nearly unarmed. Its solitary deep-pink flowers develop into elongated pendent red hips.
Mountains of central and southern Europe, woodland edges and cool slopes.
Deciduous shrub 0.5–2.5 m tall; stems upright, sparsely prickly or unarmed.
Alternate leaves with 7–11 elongated toothed leaflets, often glandular along the teeth.
Solitary pink to purplish-red flowers; sepals reflex after flowering.
Red oblong pendent hip, often with persistent calyx.
Boxleaf plocosperma
Plocosperma buxifolium
boxleaf plocosperma
Mesoamerican shrub, sole member of a distinct family. Opposite leathery leaves contrast with purple tubular flowers and hairy seeds.
Dry forests and edges from Mexico to Costa Rica, often on rocky ground.
Branched shrub or small tree, usually a few meters tall.
Leaves simple, opposite, leathery, elliptic, with entire margins.
Bisexual flowers with a funnel-shaped corolla, usually five-lobed and often purple.
Elongated two-valved capsule; seeds carry long silky hairs.
Blue-flowered setchellanthus
Setchellanthus caeruleus
blue-flowered setchellanthus
Aromatic shrub of Mexican arid scrub, sole known member of Setchellanthaceae. Its large blue-violet axillary flowers have numerous floral parts.
Endemic to Mexico in dry scrub and semiarid areas.
Aromatic branched shrub 1–3 m tall.
Leaves simple, alternate, small, elliptic, and entire.
Large blue-violet axillary flowers with numerous floral parts.
Dry seed capsule, unlike a silique.
Creeping devil cactus
Stenocereus eruca
creeping devil cactus
Creeping cactus endemic to Baja California. Spiny stems lie on sand and advance from a raised tip; the rear portions may die.
Baja California Sur, especially sandy coastal plains around Magdalena Bay.
Prostrate cactus with cylindrical stems several meters long that root adventitiously.
Leaves absent; succulent ribbed stems bear spiny areoles.
Nocturnal white to pinkish flowers near the raised stem tips.
Fleshy reddish berry with deciduous spines or bristles.
Cape retzia
Retzia capensis
Cape retzia
Small shrub endemic to Cape fynbos. Narrow leaves and red-orange tubular flowers with dark, hairy tips are distinctive.
Western Cape, South Africa; slopes and sandstone outcrops.
Erect, densely leafy shrublet, generally up to 1.5 m.
Leaves alternate, narrow, simple, leathery, and entire.
Red-orange tubular flowers in clusters, with dark tips and tufts of white hairs.
Small dry capsule after flowering.
Panicle terminalia
Terminalia paniculata
panicle terminalia
Large tree of moist deciduous forests in peninsular India. Leaves may bear basal glands; small greenish flowers develop into an unequal-winged fruit.
Peninsular India, including the Western Ghats and neighboring regions.
Deciduous tree about 12–16 m tall, with straight trunk and spreading crown.
Leaves simple, alternate, lanceolate to oblong; glands sometimes near petiole base.
Small greenish flowers in axillary or terminal racemes.
Compressed reddish-brown samara with three unequal wings, the middle one largest.
Abarema turbinata
Abarema turbinata
Jupunba turbinata
Small coastal Brazilian tree published as Abarema turbinata, a synonym of Jupunba turbinata according to Kew. Long stamens project beyond the flowers; the mature pod twists.
Endemic to coastal Atlantic forest in Bahia, in sandy formations.
Tree or large shrub 3–4.5 m tall.
Alternate bipinnate leaves, often with one pair of pinnae and large leaflets.
Flowers in heads or racemes; long white stamens project conspicuously.
Compressed, reticulate, spirally twisted pod containing several seeds.
Java coral tree
Erythrina euodiphylla
Java coral tree
Erythrina of Java and the Lesser Sunda Islands, often flowering on nearly bare branches. Trifoliolate leaves and purple seeds distinguish it from close relatives with red seeds.
Eastern Java, Bali, and Timor; Kew includes the Lesser Sunda Islands in its range.
Spiny tree or shrub, deciduous or briefly leafless at flowering.
Alternate trifoliolate leaf with broadly elliptic leaflets.
Red-orange papilionoid flowers in clusters; the consulted source reports color at genus level.
Elongated pod constricted between seeds; purple seeds according to the published taxonomic comparison.
Chinese rhoiptelea
Rhoiptelea chiliantha
Chinese rhoiptelea
Tree of southern China and northern Vietnam with long pendent panicles. Axes and young parts carry pale yellow glandular hairs.
Southeastern China and northern Vietnam; montane forests.
Tree reaching about 20 m.
Alternate pinnate leaf with 7–13 toothed leaflets; rachis glandular.
Small greenish flowers in long loose pendent panicles.
Very small nutlet with four ribs and four rounded wings.
Alonso’s turbinicarpus
Turbinicarpus alonsoi
Alonso’s turbinicarpus
Small globose Mexican cactus with a very restricted range and critically endangered status. Prominent tubercles and a large pink terminal flower are characteristic.
Guanajuato, Mexico; very restricted range on calcareous substrate.
Low solitary cactus, about 5–12 cm across, partly sunken.
Globose stem with spiral tubercles; areoles bear short pale spines.
Large funnel-shaped pink to magenta flower at the stem apex.
Small dry capsule; seeds are dark.
Sansevieria forskaliana
Sansevieria forskaliana
Forsskål’s sansevieria
Sansevieria forskaliana is retained as the tree name; Kew treats the taxon as Dracaena forskaliana. Rhizomatous rosette with rigid mottled leaves, raceme, and berries.
Northeastern Africa and Arabian Peninsula, in dry scrub and savanna.
Stemless perennial rosette herb with underground rhizome.
Rigid upright lance-shaped mottled leaves, hard brown tip, and pale marginal stripe.
Upright raceme of whitish tubular flowers in small clusters.
Orange berry containing one to three seeds.
Yellow bivonaea
Bivonaea lutea
yellow bivonaea
Tiny Mediterranean annual in Brassicaceae. A rosette of oblong leaves precedes a slender stem with small yellow flowers; short silicles are net-veined.
Southern Italy, Sicily, Malta, and central Mediterranean, mostly dry habitats.
Annual only a few centimeters tall, generally 4–22 cm.
Basal oblong toothed leaves; smaller alternate stem leaves.
Small four-petalled yellow flowers in a terminal raceme.
Compressed oblong silicle only a few millimeters long, with netted cross-veins.
Lemaire’s melon cactus
Melocactus lemarii
Lemaire’s melon cactus
Globose Caribbean cactus bearing a reddish woolly cephalium at the apex. Small flowers emerge from the cephalium, distinguishing the genus from cacti without one.
Eastern Caribbean, including Hispaniola; dry rocky habitats.
Solitary globose to short-cylindrical cactus, topped at maturity by a cephalium.
Ribbed stem with spiny areoles; apical cephalium covered in wool and bristles.
Small pink tubular flowers produced from the cephalium.
Oblong red berry emerging from the cephalium at maturity.
